title: Abecedarian Children Grow Up
text:
In the 1970s, the Abecedarian Project in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, enrolled infants born into disadvantaged families, most of them African American. Half were randomly chosen to receive an intensive program that began in the first months of life and continued until age five: full-day childcare focused on language, play and learning, along with nutrition and basic health care. The other half received nutritional supplements and the usual support available in the community.

Early reports focused on what the program did for intelligence and schooling. Children who took part had higher test scores and were more likely to attend college. But the researchers kept following them.

In 2014, a team led by Frances Campbell and the economist James Heckman published a study in Science looking at the participants' health in their mid-thirties. Doctors examined them, measured their blood pressure and weight and took blood samples. Those who had received the early childhood program had markedly lower risk of heart and metabolic disease than the control group. The differences were especially clear among the men, who had lower blood pressure and much less metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risk factors for heart disease and diabetes.

The study suggested that early care can shape not only learning but the body itself, decades later.
lesson: What a child receives in the first five years can protect health into middle age. Early care is one of the best long-term investments a family or a society can make.
people: Frances Campbell, Gabriella Conti, James Heckman and colleagues
source: Campbell, F., Conti, G., Heckman, J. J., Moon, S. H., Pinto, R., Pungello, E., and Pan, Y. (2014). Early childhood investments substantially boost adult health. Science, 343(6178), 1478-1485.
caveat: The health follow-up involved a small number of participants, so the precise sizes of the effects are uncertain.
